title: On Succinct Obfuscation via Propositional Proofs
authors: Abhishek Jain (NTT Research and John Hopkins University), Zhengzhong Jin (Northeastern University), Surya Mathialagan (NTT Research), Omer Paneth (Tel Aviv University)
abstract: A central goal in the study of indistinguishability obfuscation (IO) is to minimize the size of the obfuscation. Existing results show how to obfuscate programs represented as Turing machines such that the size of the obfuscation depends only on the input length and not on the machine's running time. Jain and Jin (FOCS 2022) further showed how to eliminate even this input-length dependency for functionally equivalent programs whose equivalence can be proven in Cook's theory PV. In this work, we explore the limits of achieving fully succinct obfuscation. We study the setting where a program has a large description, most of which can be public while only a small portion remains secret. We introduce a new notion of fully succinct IO, in which the size of the obfuscated program depends only on the size of the secret part, and not on the public part or on the input length. Starting from input-succinct IO for PV-equivalent machines—known to follow from super-polynomially secure IO for circuits and the Learning with Errors (LWE) assumption—we construct fully succinct IO for the same class of programs, which we call fully succinct PV-IO. We then show how to bootstrap fully succinct PV-IO to achieve full IO security. Our bootstrapping theorems rely on succinct cryptographic primitives with seemingly weaker functionality: either succinct witness encryption or SNARGs for NP with unique proofs. We also require that the correctness of these primitives be provable in theory PV, and we show that these assumptions are both sufficient and necessary. Finally, we demonstrate several applications of fully succinct IO and PV-IO: (i) we give the first IO construction where the size of the obfuscated program is less than twice the size of the original program for a large class of useful programs; (ii) we show how to avoid the need for padding programs prior to obfuscation—often required in existing analyses—by replacing the padding with a public random string; and (iii) we present the first construction of succinct computational secret sharing for access structures represented by polynomial-size monotone circuits, where the share size does not grow with the size of the access structure.
